questions.question: A service calls Claude for every request and reuses an identical 12,000-token instruction block each time. Latency and cost are both too high. What is the most direct improvement?

options.A: Batch requests together and process them hourly
options.B: Shorten the instructions until the cost is acceptable
options.C: Cache the stable prefix so the repeated block is not reprocessed on every call
options.D: Move to a smaller model

questions.rationale: A large, unchanging prefix is exactly what prompt caching exists for, and it cuts both cost and time to first token without changing behavior. Trimming instructions (B) sacrifices capability, a smaller model (D) trades quality for price, and batching (A) breaks a per-request service.

questions.question: A user-facing feature must show output as it is produced rather than after a long wait. What does this require?

options.A: A smaller model so the whole response arrives sooner
options.B: Splitting the prompt into several shorter calls
options.C: Streaming the response so tokens are delivered as they are generated
options.D: Reducing the maximum output tokens

questions.rationale: Streaming is the mechanism for incremental delivery and is what perceived latency depends on. A smaller model (A) and a shorter cap (D) reduce total time without changing when the first token appears, and splitting (B) adds round trips.

questions.question: Ten thousand documents must be classified overnight, with no interactive requirement. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Splitting the job across several API keys
options.B: Running them in parallel at maximum concurrency against the standard endpoint
options.C: Streaming requests one at a time to show progress
options.D: Submitting the work as a batch, accepting higher latency for lower cost

questions.rationale: Work that is large, uniform, and not time-critical is what batch processing is for, and it is materially cheaper. Streaming (C) serves interactive use, maximum concurrency (B) risks rate limits for no benefit here, and splitting keys (A) is an evasion rather than a design.

questions.question: An integration intermittently receives a rate limit response under load. What is the correct handling?

options.A: Retry immediately until the call succeeds
options.B: Lower the request size so the limit is never reached
options.C: Retry with exponential backoff and a bounded number of attempts
options.D: Treat the response as a permanent failure and surface an error

questions.rationale: Backoff with a retry ceiling relieves the pressure that caused the limit and still fails predictably. Immediate retries (A) worsen the condition, treating it as terminal (D) discards recoverable work, and shrinking requests (B) does not address a rate that is measured in calls.

questions.question: Output must be inserted directly into a typed database record. What is the most reliable way to obtain it?

options.A: Post-process the prose into fields with regular expressions
options.B: Ask for JSON and retry when parsing fails
options.C: Define the shape as a tool schema so the response is returned in a validated structure
options.D: Ask for JSON in the prompt and parse whatever comes back

questions.rationale: A declared schema turns structure into a contract the response must satisfy, which is what a typed insert needs. Asking in prose (D) and retrying on failure (B) both leave the shape to chance, and regular expressions over prose (A) are brittle by construction.

questions.question: A long-running conversation eventually exceeds the context window. What is the appropriate design response?

options.A: Increase the maximum output tokens
options.B: Summarise earlier turns into a compact running state and carry that forward
options.C: Truncate the oldest turns and continue
options.D: Start a new conversation with no history

questions.rationale: Compaction preserves the meaning of earlier exchanges within a much smaller footprint, which is what continuity requires. Blind truncation (C) drops facts silently, the output cap (A) is unrelated, and starting fresh (D) discards the state entirely.

questions.question: Which signal best indicates that a failed request should not be retried?

options.A: The same request failed once before
options.B: The error indicates a malformed request rather than a transient condition
options.C: The account is near its spending limit
options.D: The response took longer than usual

questions.rationale: A client error means the request itself is wrong, and repeating it unchanged cannot succeed. Latency (D) and a single prior failure (A) are consistent with transient faults, and a spending limit (C) is an operational matter rather than a property of the request.

questions.question: A response is truncated mid-sentence. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The input exceeded the context window
options.B: The model does not support the requested format
options.C: The network connection dropped
options.D: The output reached the maximum token limit set on the request

questions.rationale: Hitting the output cap produces exactly this symptom and is reported as such in the stop reason. An oversized input (A) fails before generation, an unsupported format (B) produces wrong shape rather than a cut, and a dropped connection (C) is an error rather than a clean stop.

questions.question: A high-volume classification task is currently handled by the largest available model with near-perfect accuracy. What should be evaluated?

options.A: Whether a smaller model reaches the accuracy the task actually requires at lower cost
options.B: Nothing, since accuracy is the only goal
options.C: Whether the prompt can be lengthened to improve accuracy further
options.D: Whether the task can be run less frequently

questions.rationale: Model selection is a fit-to-requirement decision, and a simple, repetitive task is where a smaller model most often suffices. Treating accuracy as unbounded (B) ignores cost, a longer prompt (C) adds expense for no stated need, and reducing frequency (D) changes the requirement rather than meeting it.

questions.question: Which task most clearly justifies the most capable model available?

options.A: Extracting a date from a short, well-formed string
options.B: Deciding a multi-step migration plan across several interacting systems
options.C: Converting a list into title case
options.D: Detecting whether a message is in English

questions.rationale: Deep, multi-step reasoning over interacting constraints is where capability differences show. The other three are mechanical or single-signal tasks that a small model handles at a fraction of the cost.

questions.question: Cost has risen sharply while request volume is flat. What should be inspected first?

options.A: The average response time
options.B: Token usage per request, including how much context is resent each call
options.C: The number of API keys in use
options.D: The model's published price

questions.rationale: With volume flat, cost per request must have grown, and context sent per call is the usual driver. Published price (D) would be a known change, key count (C) does not affect cost, and latency (A) is not billed.

questions.question: What is the correct way to decide between two models for a specific task?

options.A: Choose the larger model and reduce cost elsewhere
options.B: Measure both against a representative sample of the real task and its quality bar
options.C: Choose the newer model, since it supersedes the older one
options.D: Choose the one with the better published benchmark scores

questions.rationale: Model choice is empirical and task-specific, which is what a representative evaluation establishes. Benchmarks (D) may not reflect the task, recency (C) is not a measurement, and defaulting to size (A) decides before evidence.

questions.question: A process has fixed, known steps in a fixed order, each with a checkable output. What should be built?

options.A: A multi-agent system with one agent per step
options.B: A deterministic workflow that calls the model at defined points
options.C: An agent that decides the order at runtime
options.D: A single prompt containing all the steps

questions.rationale: When the path is known in advance, encoding it directly is cheaper, faster, and far easier to debug than letting a model rediscover it each run. Runtime decisions (A, C) add nondeterminism with no benefit, and a single prompt (D) removes the checkpoints between steps.

questions.question: What most reliably distinguishes a task that genuinely needs an agent?

options.A: The steps required cannot be known until intermediate results are seen
options.B: The output must be structured
options.C: The task is long
options.D: The task involves several different tools

questions.rationale: Agents earn their cost where the path must be discovered during execution. Length (C), tool count (D), and structured output (B) are all satisfied by a fixed workflow.

questions.question: A subagent is introduced to a working pipeline and quality drops. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The pipeline needs more subagents
options.B: Subagents are unsuitable for pipelines
options.C: The subagent needs a larger model
options.D: The subagent lacks context the main agent held, and the handoff did not carry it

questions.rationale: Delegation trades context for isolation, and quality falls when the handoff omits what the subtask needed. A larger model (C) cannot supply missing context, subagents are widely used in pipelines (B), and adding more (A) multiplies the same fault.

questions.question: What is the primary reason to give an agent a hard step limit?

options.A: To bound the damage and expense when the agent fails to converge
options.B: To reduce the cost of a successful run
options.C: To simplify the prompt
options.D: To make the agent respond faster

questions.rationale: A step ceiling is a safety bound for the non-terminating case, which is the failure mode that matters. Successful runs (B) usually finish well inside the limit, and neither speed (D) nor prompt clarity (C) is what the limit governs.

questions.question: Which change most improves reliability when a prompt must follow several constraints at once?

options.A: Adding emphasis to the most important constraint
options.B: Repeating the constraints at the end of the prompt
options.C: Raising the temperature so the model explores more options
options.D: Giving the model an example of a compliant output

questions.rationale: A worked example makes the constraints concrete and demonstrates their interaction, which prose cannot. Emphasis (A) and repetition (B) restate without clarifying, and higher temperature (C) increases variance, which is the opposite of reliability.

questions.question: Where should stable, reusable instructions about role and behavior be placed?

options.A: Repeated in every user message
options.B: In the final message, so they are freshest
options.C: In the system prompt, so they apply consistently across the exchange
options.D: In the first user message of every conversation

questions.rationale: The system prompt is the designated place for persistent framing and keeps it separate from turn-specific content. Placing it in user turns (A, B, D) mixes configuration with input and invites drift.

questions.question: A prompt includes a large volume of loosely related background in case it helps. What is the likely effect?

options.A: The model ignores anything not referenced by the question
options.B: Relevant material competes with irrelevant material, and accuracy can fall
options.C: Only cost is affected
options.D: Accuracy improves because more context is always better

questions.rationale: Context is a budget rather than a free resource, and irrelevant material dilutes attention to what matters. More is not automatically better (D), the model does not reliably filter for you (A), and the effect is on quality as well as cost (C).

questions.question: What most determines whether a model calls a tool correctly?

options.A: How clearly the tool's description and parameters state what it does and when to use it
options.B: Whether the tool returns JSON
options.C: The order the tools are declared in
options.D: The number of tools available

questions.rationale: A tool description is the model's only guide to selection and use, so it is where correctness is won or lost. Tool count (D) and declaration order (C) matter far less, and the return format (B) affects consumption rather than selection.

questions.question: An MCP server exposes forty overlapping tools and the model frequently picks the wrong one. What is the best remedy?

options.A: Increase the context window
options.B: Consolidate and sharpen the tool surface so each tool has a distinct purpose
options.C: Add instructions telling the model to choose carefully
options.D: Present the tools in alphabetical order

questions.rationale: Ambiguity between tools is a design problem in the interface and is fixed by making each tool distinct. Instructions (C) do not resolve genuine overlap, context size (A) is not the constraint, and ordering (D) does not clarify purpose.

questions.question: What is the correct handling when a tool call returns an error?

options.A: Retry the identical call until it succeeds
options.B: Abandon the run
options.C: Return the error to the model as a tool result so it can adapt
options.D: Return the raw error to the end user

questions.rationale: Feeding the error back keeps the model in the loop and lets it correct its arguments or choose another path. Raw errors (D) leak internals, blind retries (A) repeat the fault, and abandoning (B) discards recoverable runs.

questions.question: A document fetched from the web contains text instructing the model to ignore prior instructions. What is the correct architecture?

options.A: Filter for the phrase before processing
options.B: Add a prompt instruction telling the model to ignore embedded instructions
options.C: Use a larger model, which is less susceptible
options.D: Treat all fetched content as data, and enforce permissions outside the model

questions.rationale: Retrieved content is untrusted input, and the durable defense is that the model's authority is limited by the surrounding system rather than by its own compliance. Prompt instructions (B), phrase filters (A), and model size (C) are all bypassable.

questions.question: What is the appropriate way to give an integration access to a database?

options.A: Provide full credentials so the model can handle any request
options.B: Provide access through a tool with no schema so it stays flexible
options.C: Provide read and write access but instruct the model to avoid writes
options.D: Expose only the specific operations the task requires, scoped to what it may touch

questions.rationale: Least privilege bounds the consequences of any mistake or manipulation, and it is enforced outside the prompt. Full credentials (A) and instruction-based restraint (C) rely on behavior rather than control, and an unscoped tool (B) removes the boundary.

questions.question: A change to a prompt appears to improve output on the three examples you tried. What should happen before it ships?

options.A: Run it against a held-out set that represents the real distribution and compare on defined criteria
options.B: Ask the model whether the new prompt is better
options.C: Ship it behind a flag and watch for complaints
options.D: Ship it, since three examples agreed

questions.rationale: Three hand-picked examples cannot distinguish a real improvement from noise, which is what an evaluation set exists to settle. Self-assessment (B) is not measurement, and shipping first (C, D) makes users the test set.

questions.question: Your service makes a Messages API call and the response carries stop_reason "end_turn" with a tool_use block absent. What does your loop do?

options.A: Append an empty tool result and continue the loop
options.B: Treat the turn as complete and return the content to the caller
options.C: Execute the last requested tool again
options.D: Re-send the request with higher max_tokens

questions.rationale: "end_turn" means the model has finished; "tool_use" is the signal to execute a tool and continue the loop

questions.question: A nightly job enriches 200,000 product descriptions. Results are consumed the next morning. Which design minimizes cost?

options.A: Synchronous calls fanned out across many workers
options.B: Synchronous calls with a smaller model and reduced max_tokens
options.C: One request containing all descriptions
options.D: The Message Batches API with results collected within its processing window

questions.rationale: Latency-tolerant bulk work is the Batches API's purpose: 50% of the cost within a 24-hour window

questions.question: Which change makes a repeated 10,000-token system prompt cheaper and faster without losing content?

options.A: Compressing the prompt text with abbreviations
options.B: Moving the prompt to the end of the request
options.C: Sending the prompt only on the first request of a session
options.D: Placing the stable prompt first and enabling prompt caching so the prefix is reused

questions.rationale: Caching reuses a stable prefix, cutting time-to-first-token and per-request cost. Position matters: stable content first

questions.question: Your extraction endpoint occasionally receives JSON with a missing required field, and downstream code throws. What is the sturdiest production pattern?

options.A: Wrap the parse in a try block and return an empty object on failure
options.B: Post-process with a regular expression that inserts missing fields
options.C: Instruct the model more firmly in the system prompt
options.D: Enforce a schema through tool use, validate the parsed result, and retry once with the validation error appended

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop treats model output as untrusted input and lets the model self-correct

questions.question: A teammate proposes an autonomous agent for a pipeline whose five steps are identical for every input. What is the strongest technical objection?

options.A: Agents cannot call tools reliably
options.B: Agents are unsupported in production
options.C: The pipeline would need a larger context window
options.D: A known, fixed path does not need model-chosen control flow; deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable

questions.rationale: Autonomy is justified when the path is unknown. A fixed path belongs in deterministic code that can be tested

questions.question: Which is the correct use of a subagent in an agent system?

options.A: To isolate a self-contained subtask so its verbose intermediate context does not fill the parent's window
options.B: To provide a fallback if the main model is unavailable
options.C: To run the same prompt twice for consensus
options.D: To bypass rate limits

questions.rationale: Subagents delegate and isolate context; that isolation is their main architectural value

questions.question: An agent that summarizes user-submitted URLs must never be able to trigger a refund. Where is that guaranteed?

options.A: By instructing the model to confirm before refunds
options.B: In the system prompt, stated clearly
options.C: By not granting the agent the refund tool, and enforcing that with tool configuration or hooks
options.D: By using a model known for instruction following

questions.rationale: Capability the agent does not hold cannot be misused. Prompts and confirmations are not enforcement

questions.question: Your team pins model versions in production. What is the primary reason?

options.A: Pinning is required by the API
options.B: Model updates can change behavior, so upgrades become deliberate, evaluated changes rather than surprises
options.C: Pinning increases the context window
options.D: Pinned models are cheaper

questions.rationale: Pinning makes model behavior a controlled dependency so upgrades pass through evaluation

questions.question: Which describes the correct relationship between an MCP server and the applications that use it?

options.A: Each application embeds its own copy of the server code
options.B: The server replaces the Messages API
options.C: The server must run in the same process as the model
options.D: The server exposes tools and resources that multiple clients connect to, maintained independently of any one application

questions.rationale: An MCP server is a reusable, independently maintained capability that multiple clients share

questions.question: A long-running assistant begins contradicting itself and forgetting recent constraints. Inspection shows the context is nearly full of verbose tool outputs. What is the correct remedy?

options.A: Repeat the system prompt after every turn
options.B: Reduce max_tokens on each response
options.C: Increase temperature to encourage variety
options.D: Prune and summarize tool outputs, compact history, and isolate subtasks so the working context stays lean

questions.rationale: Context drift and bloat are managed by pruning, compaction, and isolation

questions.question: When is few-shot prompting the right tool?

options.A: When the model needs more factual knowledge
options.B: When the context window is too small
options.C: When output format or edge-case handling is inconsistent and examples can demonstrate the target behavior
options.D: When latency must be reduced

questions.rationale: Few-shot examples fix format and edge-case behavior far better than more instructions

questions.question: A page retrieved by your agent contains hidden text instructing it to reveal its system prompt. Which mitigation actually works?

options.A: Treating retrieved content as untrusted data, separating it from instructions, and gating sensitive capabilities behind guardrails
options.B: Asking the model in the system prompt to ignore such instructions
options.C: Filtering pages that contain the word "ignore"
options.D: Raising temperature so behavior is less predictable

questions.rationale: Injection defense is structural: separate untrusted content and apply least privilege to consequential tools

questions.question: Which statement about the Message Batches API is correct?

options.A: It requires a dedicated endpoint per request
options.B: It guarantees sub-second latency
options.C: It processes large asynchronous workloads at reduced cost within a processing window, correlating requests by custom_id
options.D: It supports multi-turn tool calling within a batch

questions.rationale: Reduced cost, asynchronous window, custom_id correlation, and no multi-turn tool calling inside a batch

questions.question: Your CI pipeline runs Claude Code non-interactively and must parse its output. Which invocation fits?

options.A: Interactive mode with output piped to a file
options.B: The print flag with a JSON output format and a schema, so results are machine-readable and validated
options.C: A wrapper that screen-scrapes the terminal
options.D: Plan mode with a human approver

questions.rationale: Headless CI use means non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output

questions.question: Traces show your assistant reasons correctly over the documents it receives, but frequently receives documents unrelated to the question. Where is the defect?

options.A: The output parser
options.B: The system prompt, which needs stronger accuracy language
options.C: The model, which should be upgraded
options.D: The retrieval layer that selects the documents

questions.rationale: Traces localize the fault to the integration layer: correct reasoning over wrong inputs is a retrieval defect

questions.question: A service sends the same 8,000-token system prompt on every request and cost is dominated by input tokens. What is the first change to evaluate?

options.A: Switching to a cheaper model
options.B: Reducing the number of requests
options.C: Caching the stable prefix so it is not reprocessed on every call
options.D: Rewriting the system prompt to be shorter

questions.rationale: A large unchanging prefix repeated per call is what caching addresses, without losing any instruction. Shortening (D) sacrifices capability, a cheaper model (A) trades quality, and fewer requests (B) changes the product

questions.question: An endpoint must return within 500 ms but the model needs longer for a good answer. What is the appropriate pattern?

options.A: Use the smallest model regardless of quality
options.B: Return an acknowledgement immediately and deliver the result through a callback or poll
options.C: Truncate the model's output
options.D: Increase the timeout on the client

questions.rationale: Decoupling acceptance from completion satisfies the latency contract without degrading the answer. Truncation (C) and a minimal model (A) sacrifice the result, and the timeout (D) is the stated constraint

questions.question: What does a stop reason indicating the maximum token limit tell you?

options.A: The input was too long
options.B: The model refused the request
options.C: The request was malformed
options.D: The output was cut off before the model finished

questions.rationale: That stop reason reports that generation hit the output ceiling. An oversized input (A) fails before generation, and neither a malformed request (C) nor a refusal (B) produces this reason

questions.question: A tool result returns 50,000 tokens of JSON, most of it unused. What is the right fix?

options.A: Raise the model's context limit
options.B: Call the tool less frequently
options.C: Change the tool to return only the fields the task needs
options.D: Summarise the JSON with a second model call

questions.rationale: Tools should return what the task requires, which preserves context for reasoning. A larger window (A) delays the problem, a second call (D) adds cost and failure surface, and calling less often (B) does not change the payload

questions.question: Which condition warrants a retry with backoff rather than surfacing an error?

options.A: The request contained an invalid parameter
options.B: The response exceeded the expected length
options.C: The service returned a rate limit or a transient server error
options.D: The model returned an answer you disagree with

questions.rationale: Rate limits and transient server errors are the recoverable class. An invalid parameter (A) will fail identically, and disagreement (D) or length (B) are not transport failures

questions.question: A workload runs nightly over 50,000 records with no interactive requirement. Which choice reduces cost most?

options.A: Submitting the work as a batch
options.B: Using the largest model for accuracy
options.C: Streaming each request
options.D: Increasing concurrency against the standard endpoint

questions.rationale: Large, uniform, latency-tolerant work is exactly the batch case, and it is materially cheaper. Streaming (C) serves interactive use, the largest model (B) raises cost, and concurrency (D) does not change unit price

questions.question: Accuracy on a simple extraction task is identical between a small and a large model. What should be deployed?

options.A: The newest model available
options.B: The large model, in case inputs change
options.C: Both, alternating between them
options.D: The small model, since it meets the requirement at lower cost

questions.rationale: Where the requirement is met, the cheaper option is correct, and changing inputs are handled by re-evaluating. Insurance against hypothetical change (B), alternation (C), and recency (A) all spend without benefit

questions.question: A task requires the model to plan across many interacting constraints and revise as it goes. What does this argue for?

options.A: Splitting the task across several small models
options.B: The smallest model, to keep cost down
options.C: A longer prompt with the same model
options.D: A more capable model, since the work is reasoning-heavy

questions.rationale: Multi-step reasoning under interacting constraints is where capability differences show. A small model (B) and splitting (A) both fragment the reasoning, and prompt length (C) does not add capability

questions.question: An agent is given ten tools, three of which overlap in purpose. What is the likely consequence?

options.A: Better error handling
options.B: More frequent wrong tool selection
options.C: Lower token cost
options.D: Faster execution, since more options are available

questions.rationale: Overlapping tools make selection ambiguous, which is where agents go wrong. Overlap does not improve speed (D), reduce cost (C), or help error handling (A)

questions.question: Where should a stable instruction that must apply to every turn be placed?

options.A: In the system prompt
options.B: At the end of the latest user message
options.C: Repeated in each user message
options.D: In a tool description

questions.rationale: The system prompt is designed for persistent framing across the exchange. Placing it in user turns (B, C) mixes configuration with input, and tool descriptions (D) govern tool selection

questions.question: Which change most improves output that is correct but inconsistently formatted?

options.A: Asking for the output to be neat
options.B: Providing an example of the exact output required
options.C: Raising the temperature
options.D: Using a larger model

questions.rationale: An example defines the target unambiguously, which is what formatting consistency needs. Higher temperature (C) increases variance, a vague adjective (A) does not specify, and a larger model (D) does not know your format

questions.question: What is the most important property of a tool description?

options.A: It lists the implementation language
options.B: It states what the tool does, when to use it, and what each parameter means
options.C: It is short
options.D: It matches the function name exactly

questions.rationale: The description is the model's only basis for choosing and calling the tool correctly. Brevity (C) is secondary to clarity, and implementation detail (A) and naming (D) do not guide selection

questions.question: Content retrieved from an external site contains instructions aimed at the model. What is the correct defense?

options.A: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data and bound the model's permissions outside the prompt
options.B: Instruct the model in the system prompt to ignore such content
options.C: Scan for known injection phrases and block them
options.D: Use a model with a larger context window

questions.rationale: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its granted permissions regardless of what the content says. Prompt instructions (B) and phrase filters (C) are bypassable, and context size (D) is irrelevant

questions.question: A prompt change improved results on the five examples you tested. What should happen before it reaches production?

options.A: Ship it, since all five improved
options.B: Ship it to a small percentage of traffic and watch error rates
options.C: Ask the model to compare the two prompts
options.D: Evaluate it against a held-out set that reflects real inputs, on defined criteria

questions.rationale: Five hand-picked cases cannot separate a real gain from noise, which is what an evaluation set settles. Self-comparison (C) is not measurement, and shipping first (A, B) makes users the test

questions.question: A request fails with an authentication error after working for months. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: A credential that expired, was rotated, or lost its permissions
options.B: A transient service fault
options.C: The prompt became too long
options.D: The model was deprecated

questions.rationale: Authentication failures point at the credential rather than the payload. A transient fault (B) presents differently, and neither prompt length (C) nor deprecation (D) produces an auth error

questions.question: What is the purpose of correlating a request identifier through an integration?

options.A: It is required by the API
options.B: It improves model accuracy
options.C: It reduces token cost
options.D: It lets a specific response be traced back to the request that produced it

questions.rationale: Correlation exists for traceability, which is what debugging asynchronous or batched work depends on. It does not affect cost (C) or accuracy (B), and it is a design practice rather than a requirement (A)

questions.question: An integration must handle a response that stops early because the model called a tool. What does the application do next?

options.A: Return the partial text to the user
options.B: Treat it as an error and retry
options.C: Increase the output token limit
options.D: Execute the tool and return its result so the model can continue

questions.rationale: A tool-use stop is a handoff, and the loop continues once the result is returned. Retrying (B) repeats the request, returning partial text (A) discards the work, and the token limit (C) is unrelated

questions.question: Which is the strongest reason to put a queue between an application and the model?

options.A: It makes responses more accurate
options.B: It absorbs bursts so load stays within rate limits without dropping work
options.C: It reduces the token count
options.D: It removes the need for retries

questions.rationale: A queue smooths demand against a rate-limited dependency. It does not change accuracy (A) or token counts (C), and retries remain necessary (D)

questions.question: A response arrives well-formed but semantically wrong for the input. Where should investigation start?

options.A: The rate limit configuration
options.B: The output token limit
options.C: The transport layer
options.D: The prompt and the exact context supplied for that input

questions.rationale: A well-formed but wrong answer points at what the model was told, not how it was delivered. Transport (C), limits (A), and output caps (B) produce failures of delivery rather than of meaning

questions.question: What is the practical consequence of choosing a model with a much larger context window than the task needs?

options.A: Fewer rate limit errors
options.B: Better accuracy on every task
options.C: More reliable structured output
options.D: Cost and latency that the task does not require

questions.rationale: Unused capacity is paid for in cost and time. A larger window does not itself improve accuracy (B), reduce rate limiting (A), or make structure more reliable (C)

questions.question: How should a team decide when to move a task to a smaller model?

options.A: When measurement shows the smaller model meets the task's stated quality bar
options.B: When the task becomes high volume
options.C: When the budget is exceeded
options.D: When latency becomes a complaint

questions.rationale: The decision is evidence-led against a defined bar. Budget (C), volume (B), and latency (D) create pressure to look, but they do not establish that quality holds

questions.question: A long-running agent needs to keep a decision it made twenty steps ago. What is the correct mechanism?

options.A: Write it into an explicit state that is carried forward regardless of compaction
options.B: Restart the agent periodically
options.C: Increase the temperature
options.D: Rely on the context window retaining it

questions.rationale: Durable state must be explicit, because context is finite and compaction is lossy. Relying on the window (D) fails at length, temperature (C) is unrelated, and restarting (B) loses the decision

questions.question: What distinguishes a workflow from an agent in practice?

options.A: Workflows cannot call the model
options.B: In a workflow the control flow is fixed in advance; in an agent the model chooses the next step
options.C: Agents cannot use tools
options.D: Workflows are shorter

questions.rationale: Who decides the next step is the distinction that matters. Length (D) is incidental, agents do use tools (C), and workflows do call the model (A)

questions.question: A prompt contains an instruction that contradicts an example in the same prompt. What is the likely outcome?

options.A: Behavior becomes unpredictable between the two
options.B: The instruction always wins
options.C: The request is rejected
options.D: The example always wins

questions.rationale: Contradictory signals produce inconsistent behavior rather than a defined precedence. Neither the instruction (B) nor the example (D) reliably wins, and the request is not rejected (C)

questions.question: What is the effect of placing the most important instruction in the middle of a very long prompt?

options.A: It causes an error
options.B: None, position is irrelevant
options.C: It is more likely to be overlooked than if it were at a boundary
options.D: It is followed more closely

questions.rationale: Material at the edges of a long input is attended to more reliably than material buried in the middle. Position is not neutral (B) or advantageous here (D), and it does not error (A)

questions.question: When should a tool return an identifier rather than the full object?

options.A: Never, the model needs the full object
options.B: Always, to reduce cost
options.C: When the object is large and the model only needs it to make a subsequent call
options.D: Only for write operations

questions.rationale: Returning a handle keeps context free when the payload is only needed for a later call. Always returning everything (A) or nothing (B) ignores the task, and the rule is not about writes (D)

questions.question: An MCP server is added and the agent's success rate falls. What should be checked first?

options.A: The model version
options.B: Whether the new tools overlap with existing ones and have distinguishable descriptions
options.C: The network latency
options.D: The server's uptime

questions.rationale: A new tool surface most often degrades selection through overlap and unclear descriptions. Uptime (D) and latency (C) present as errors or slowness, and the model did not change (A)

questions.question: A model output will be rendered directly into a web page. What must the application do?

options.A: Treat the output as untrusted and escape or sanitise it before rendering
options.B: Nothing, model output is safe
options.C: Use a larger model
options.D: Ask the model not to produce markup

questions.rationale: Anything rendered into a page is escaped regardless of source, since output can be influenced by input. Assuming safety (B) and instructing the model (D) are not controls, and model size (C) is irrelevant

questions.question: What does a regression suite protect against that a one-off evaluation does not?

options.A: A change that improves the target behavior while quietly breaking another
options.B: Cost increases
options.C: Slow responses
options.D: Rate limits

questions.rationale: Regressions are silent by definition and are caught by continuously testing what must not break. Latency (C), limits (D), and cost (B) are operational signals rather than correctness

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT) | Adapted by the project (options and rationale reworded)
questions.question: Your support agent resolves most tickets but sometimes loops indefinitely, re-calling lookup_order on the same order. What is the correct structural fix?

options.A: Detect repeated identical calls and route to escalate_to_human when progress stalls, keeping an iteration cap only as a safety backstop
options.B: Raise max_tokens so the loop has room to finish
options.C: Lower the temperature
options.D: Remove the lookup_order tool

questions.rationale: Agent loops need engineered termination: repeated-call detection and an escalation path when the agent cannot progress, with an iteration budget as a backstop. Token budget (B) delays the symptom, removing a needed tool (D) breaks resolution, and temperature (C) does not bound iteration. Guide 1.1 names an iteration cap as the primary stop as an anti-pattern; a cap is a backstop, not the control.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: process_refund currently accepts any amount. Support policy caps agent-initiated refunds at $200; larger refunds need a human. Where does that rule belong?

options.A: Enforced in the tool layer: the tool rejects amounts over the cap with a structured error, and a hook or the tool itself routes larger cases to escalation
options.B: In the system prompt, phrased firmly
options.C: In quarterly staff training
options.D: In the model's reasoning, since it reads the policy

questions.rationale: Hard policy limits are enforced deterministically at the tool boundary, not requested of the model. Prompt phrasing (B) and model reasoning (D) are probabilistic where the requirement is absolute, and training (C) does not constrain the agent at all.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Your monorepo has frontend and backend directories with different conventions, and one team-wide rule about commit style. Where does each piece of configuration belong?

options.A: Each engineer's personal user-level CLAUDE.md
options.B: Everything in one root CLAUDE.md
options.C: The commit rule in the project-level CLAUDE.md; the per-area conventions in path-scoped rules under .claude/rules/ that load only when matching files are touched
options.D: A wiki page linked from the README

questions.rationale: The hierarchy exists for exactly this: shared rules at project scope, conditional conventions path-scoped so context is spent only where relevant. One root file (B) loads everything everywhere, personal files (A) diverge per engineer, and a wiki (D) never reaches the model.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Invoices sometimes lack a purchase-order number, and your extraction schema must handle that honestly while catching real misses. What is the right schema design?

options.A: Make everything optional to avoid validation errors
options.B: Make purchase_order nullable, so absence is recorded as null, and validate that it is present whenever the document type requires it
options.C: Make every field required so nothing is missed
options.D: Have the model invent a plausible number when one is missing

questions.rationale: Schema design encodes reality: genuinely optional data is nullable, and conditional requirements are validated downstream. All-required (C) forces fabrication or failure on legitimate documents, all-optional (A) blinds you to true misses, and invention (D) is data corruption.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Your pipeline reports 98% field accuracy, measured on the documents the schema validated cleanly. An auditor calls the number misleading. Why?

options.A: 98% is below industry standard
options.B: Accuracy should be measured only on the hardest documents
options.C: Validation-clean documents are a biased sample: the honest measure comes from a labeled sample drawn across all documents, including ones that failed or barely passed validation
options.D: Field accuracy is not a real metric

questions.rationale: Measuring only where the system already succeeded inflates the estimate; calibration requires a labeled sample representative of the full input stream. Hardest-only (B) biases in the opposite direction, the standard claim (A) is invented, and (D) is false.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Your codebase-exploration agent has get_file_contents, read_source, and fetch_file tools that all read files, and it frequently picks poorly among them. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Fine-tune the model on the tool list
options.B: Consolidate to one file-reading tool, or give the survivors sharply differentiated descriptions that state exactly when each applies
options.C: Randomize which tool the harness dispatches
options.D: Add a fourth, better file-reading tool

questions.rationale: Tool selection runs on descriptions; overlapping tools with vague descriptions produce dithering. Consolidation or sharp differentiation is the documented cure. Adding overlap (D) worsens it, fine-tuning (A) is disproportionate, and randomization (C) institutionalizes the confusion.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What is the strongest justification for splitting work across subagents?

options.A: Separate lines of work each need their own context, and mixing them degrades both
options.B: The task has many steps
options.C: The output must be assembled from several sections
options.D: Subagents are faster than a single agent

questions.rationale: Subagents exist to isolate context, so the case for them is contamination between concerns rather than volume. Step count (B) and sectioned output (C) suit a workflow, and delegation usually adds latency rather than removing it (D).
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT) | Adapted by the project (options and rationale reworded)
questions.question: An agent loops between two tools without converging. What is the most appropriate first control?

options.A: Increase the context window so it can see more history
options.B: Switch to a larger model
options.C: Define an explicit terminating condition (the loop ends on a stop_reason of end_turn, and a progress check ends it early when the same calls repeat), keeping a step ceiling only as a safety backstop
options.D: Remove one of the two tools

questions.rationale: An explicit stop condition ends the loop: end_turn, or a progress check when the same calls repeat. A step ceiling is only a backstop that contains cost if those fail. More context (A) and a larger model (B) do not guarantee convergence, and removing a tool (D) may break the task. Guide 1.1 names an iteration cap as the primary stop as an anti-pattern; a cap is a backstop, not the control.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Which property most increases the operational risk of an agentic design?

options.A: It runs longer than a minute
options.B: It calls more than one model
options.C: It produces structured output
options.D: It takes irreversible actions without a checkpoint

questions.rationale: Reversibility governs the cost of being wrong, which is the dominant risk in autonomous execution. Multiple models (B), structure (C), and duration (A) affect cost and complexity rather than blast radius.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: How should an agentic system handle a step whose result it cannot verify?

options.A: Log the step and continue
options.B: Proceed, since the model is usually right
options.C: Retry the step until two runs agree
options.D: Surface the unverifiable step for human confirmation before acting on it

questions.rationale: An unverifiable result is exactly where human judgment belongs, before it is acted upon. Assuming correctness (B) and logging without stopping (A) both act on unchecked output, and agreement across runs (C) establishes consistency rather than truth.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A team proposes an agent for a task where every input is well formed and every rule is known. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: An agent, for future flexibility
options.B: A deterministic implementation, reserving model calls for the genuinely ambiguous parts
options.C: A multi-agent design for separation of concerns
options.D: An agent with a low step limit

questions.rationale: Known rules over well-formed input are code, and using a model there buys nondeterminism at a price. Speculative flexibility (A), a constrained agent (D), and multiple agents (C) all keep the cost without the need.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What distinguishes work suited to headless mode?

options.A: It is complex and needs close supervision
options.B: It is well defined and repeatable, so it can run unattended in automation
options.C: It produces a long output
options.D: It requires many tools

questions.rationale: Headless execution suits bounded, repeatable work where no one is watching. Supervision (A) argues for interactive use, and tool count (D) and output length (C) do not determine suitability.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A skill and a subagent could both address a need. What decides between them?

options.A: Whether the task is long
options.B: Whether the need is reusable know-how or an isolated line of work with its own context
options.C: Whether the repository already has a CLAUDE.md
options.D: Skills are always preferable

questions.rationale: The two solve different problems: a skill packages reusable procedure, a subagent isolates context. A blanket preference (D), duration (A), and existing files (C) do not address that distinction.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Claude Code performs well for one engineer and inconsistently across the team. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The repository is too large
options.B: The others need more capable machines
options.C: The others are using different terminals
options.D: The working conventions live in one person's local setup rather than in the repository

questions.rationale: Context that is not committed does not travel, which produces exactly this asymmetry. Hardware (B), repository size (A), and terminal choice (C) do not explain a difference in output quality.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Which practice most improves consistency across a long-running structured extraction job?

options.A: Running each document twice
options.B: Fixing the prompt, the schema, and the model version, and recording them with the output
options.C: Increasing the output token limit
options.D: Randomising the order of documents

questions.rationale: Consistency requires that the things that shape output are pinned and recorded, so results remain comparable and reproducible. Ordering (D) is irrelevant, the token cap (C) affects length, and duplicate runs (A) measure variance without removing it.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A prompt mixes the instruction, the data, and the output format in continuous prose. What is the first improvement?

options.A: Shorten it
options.B: Move it into the system prompt
options.C: Separate the sections so the instruction, the input, and the required format are distinguishable
options.D: Add emphasis to the format requirement

questions.rationale: Structure lets the model tell instruction from data, which is the most common source of confusion in long prompts. Shortening (A) may remove needed detail, relocation (B) does not clarify, and emphasis (D) does not separate.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A tool returns a large payload that consumes most of the context window. What is the right change?

options.A: Return only what the task needs, with a way to request more detail
options.B: Summarise the payload with a second model call
options.C: Call the tool less often
options.D: Increase the context window

questions.rationale: Tools should return task-relevant results rather than everything available, which keeps context for reasoning. A larger window (D) postpones the problem, a second call (B) adds cost and a failure point, and calling less often (C) does not change the payload.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What belongs in a tool's description?

options.A: The service level agreement
options.B: What the tool does, when to use it, and what its parameters mean
options.C: The implementation language and framework
options.D: The name of the team that owns it

questions.rationale: The description is the model's selection guide, so it must answer purpose, applicability, and parameters. Implementation detail (C), service levels (A), and ownership (D) are irrelevant to the choice.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (practice) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What should be measured to know whether a production agentic system is healthy?

options.A: Task success against a defined criterion, plus the rate and shape of failures
options.B: Average response time
options.C: Total tokens consumed
options.D: The number of tool calls per run

questions.rationale: Health is defined by whether the system accomplishes the task and how it fails when it does not. Tokens (C), latency (B), and call counts (D) are cost and behavior signals that say nothing about correctness.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: The agent occasionally answers billing questions using an order it looked up three turns earlier for a different customer. What is the architectural fix?

options.A: Scope each conversation's context to one customer and clear or isolate prior lookups when the subject changes
options.B: Instruct the model to be careful about customer identity
options.C: Remove the lookup_order tool
options.D: Increase the context window

questions.rationale: Cross-customer contamination is a context-scoping defect, not a window-size problem
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: process_refund fails intermittently because the billing backend times out. What should the tool return so the agent can behave sensibly?

options.A: The exception stack trace
options.B: An empty string
options.C: A structured error with a category and a retryable flag, so the agent can retry or escalate deliberately
options.D: A message asking the user to try later

questions.rationale: Structured errors with categories and retryable flags are what let an agent recover deliberately
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Which condition should route a ticket to escalate_to_human rather than continue autonomous resolution?

options.A: The customer writes in a language the agent supports
options.B: The request falls outside documented policy, or the agent cannot make progress after a bounded number of attempts
options.C: The conversation exceeds five turns
options.D: The order is more than thirty days old

questions.rationale: Policy gaps and lack of progress are the documented escalation triggers; turn counts and order age are not
questions.review_flag: Under review: the answer key may conflict with exam guide 1.1, which calls arbitrary iteration caps an anti-pattern. Trust the official guide until content-steward rules.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: The agent sometimes calls get_customer when it should call lookup_order. What is the most effective change?

options.A: Merge them into one tool with a mode flag
options.B: Reorder the tools in the configuration
options.C: Rewrite both tool descriptions so each states precisely when it applies and how it differs from the other
options.D: Increase the model's temperature

questions.rationale: Tool selection runs on descriptions, so differentiation is the fix for confusion between similar tools
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Backend conventions should apply only when backend files are touched. Where do they belong?

options.A: In the root CLAUDE.md so they are always available
options.B: In the repository wiki
options.C: In each engineer's user-level configuration
options.D: In a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ with frontmatter matching backend paths

questions.rationale: Path-scoped rules load conditionally, which is exactly the stated requirement
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT) | Adapted by the project (options and rationale reworded)
questions.question: When is plan mode the appropriate choice over direct execution?

options.A: For every change, since planning is always safer
options.B: When the change spans many files or involves architectural choices with several valid approaches, so the codebase should be explored and the approach agreed before edits
options.C: Only when the model is unfamiliar with the language
options.D: When the context window is nearly full

questions.rationale: Exam guide task statement 3.4 (exam wording): "Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications". It lets the codebase be explored and the approach agreed before edits; simple, well-scoped changes go straight to direct execution.
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A repeated multi-step review procedure should be available to the whole team as a single invocation. What is the right mechanism?

options.A: A saved chat transcript
options.B: A longer CLAUDE.md
options.C: A shared document describing the steps
options.D: A custom slash command or skill committed to the repository

questions.rationale: Repeatable team procedures belong in committed commands or skills, not prose
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Subagents return full source documents to the coordinator, which then exceeds its context limit. What is the correct design change?

options.A: Truncate each document to its first page
options.B: Have subagents return structured findings with citations while raw sources stay at the edge or in a scratchpad
options.C: Give the coordinator a larger model
options.D: Reduce the number of subagents to one

questions.rationale: Delegation exists to keep bulk at the edge and move distilled results
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Final reports attribute claims to the wrong sources even though each subagent is individually accurate. What is the likely cause?

options.A: The search subagent returns too many results
options.B: Reports are generated before analysis completes
options.C: The synthesis model is too small
options.D: The handoff format does not carry claim and source together, so provenance is lost between stages

questions.rationale: Provenance survives handoffs only when the format carries claim and source together
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A subagent fails permanently on one source. What should the coordinator receive?

options.A: A generic failure flag with no detail
options.B: A silent retry loop until it succeeds
options.C: A propagated error with enough context to decide between retry, exclusion with a noted gap, or abort
options.D: Nothing, so the report proceeds

questions.rationale: Errors must propagate with enough context for the coordinator to choose a recovery path
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: The reviewer must emit results a pipeline can parse. Which invocation is correct?

options.A: Interactive session with output redirected to a log
options.B: Non-interactive print mode with JSON output and a schema
options.C: Plan mode with an approval step
options.D: A cron job that emails the transcript

questions.rationale: CI requires non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Reviews flag many low-value style nits and engineers now ignore them. Which change addresses this?

options.A: Define explicit review criteria and a severity bar in the prompt, with examples of in-scope and out-of-scope findings
options.B: Run the review only on large pull requests
options.C: Post findings to a separate channel
options.D: Cap output at five findings

questions.rationale: Precision comes from explicit criteria and examples that draw the signal boundary
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Some invoices legitimately lack a delivery date. How should the schema express this?

options.A: Make the field nullable so absence is recorded explicitly, with conditional validation where the document type requires it
options.B: Make the field required and let extraction fail
options.C: Omit the field from the schema
options.D: Default it to today's date

questions.rationale: Nullable fields record legitimate absence; required fields force fabrication or failure
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Which loop gives the most reliable extraction output?

options.A: Generate three times and take the majority
options.B: Generate with temperature zero and accept the result
options.C: Enforce a JSON schema through tool use, validate, and on failure retry with the validation error provided to the model
options.D: Generate, then manually review every record

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop is the reliability pattern the guide describes
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-1) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Your team reports 97% accuracy measured only on records that passed validation. Why is that number misleading?

options.A: 97% is too low to report
options.B: It excludes the failures, so it measures where the system already succeeded rather than the true rate across all documents
options.C: Validation and accuracy are unrelated
options.D: Accuracy should be measured per field, not per record

questions.rationale: Measuring only validated records is a biased sample; calibration needs coverage of all documents
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A pipeline has four steps whose order never varies and whose outputs are each checkable. What should it be?

options.A: A single prompt covering all four steps
options.B: Four agents, one per step
options.C: An agent that plans each run
options.D: A deterministic workflow with model calls at defined points

questions.rationale: A known fixed order is encoded rather than rediscovered, which is cheaper and testable per step. Runtime planning (B, C) adds nondeterminism, and one prompt (A) removes the checkpoints
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What is the principal cost of introducing a subagent?

options.A: It requires a larger model
options.B: It loses the context the parent held unless the handoff carries it explicitly
options.C: It doubles token cost in every case
options.D: It cannot use tools

questions.rationale: Delegation buys isolation and pays in context, which is why handoffs must be explicit. A subagent does not require a larger model (A), can use tools (D), and cost varies with the work (C)
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: An autonomous step would modify production data. What does the architecture require?

options.A: A longer system prompt describing caution
options.B: A more capable model
options.C: A checkpoint where a person authorises the action, or a reversible mechanism
options.D: A retry policy

questions.rationale: Irreversible external effects need an authorisation boundary or reversibility, enforced outside the model. Capability (B), instruction (A), and retries (D) do not bound the consequence
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What most helps diagnose an agentic failure after the fact?

options.A: A trace of each step's inputs, tool calls, and outputs
options.B: The final output alone
options.C: The model version
options.D: The total token count

questions.rationale: A per-step trace reconstructs a nondeterministic run, which is what diagnosis needs. The final output (B), token totals (D), and version (C) do not show where it diverged
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Where should repository-wide conventions for Claude Code live?

options.A: In the team's chat channel
options.B: In the CI configuration only
options.C: In a CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
options.D: In each developer's local configuration

questions.rationale: Committed project memory is shared, versioned, and reviewed with the code. Local configuration (D) does not propagate, chat (A) is not read as context, and CI (B) covers automation rather than interactive work
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Which task is best suited to headless Claude Code in CI?

options.A: Designing a new module's architecture
options.B: Exploratory debugging of an unfamiliar failure
options.C: A repeatable, well-specified check that runs on every pull request
options.D: Pair programming with a developer

questions.rationale: Headless execution suits bounded, repeatable work that runs unattended. Exploration (B), design (A), and pairing (D) all depend on a person in the loop
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What is a hook for?

options.A: Running a deterministic action at a defined point, independently of the model
options.B: Holding project context
options.C: Selecting the model
options.D: Storing reusable instructions

questions.rationale: Hooks execute as code at fixed points, which is how a guarantee is enforced. Instructions (D) and context (B) belong in project memory, and model choice (C) is configuration
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A pipeline needs output that always conforms to a fixed shape. What is the correct mechanism?

options.A: Lowering the temperature
options.B: Requesting the shape in the prompt and parsing the result
options.C: Post-processing prose with regular expressions
options.D: Declaring the shape as a schema the model must satisfy, and validating on receipt

questions.rationale: A declared schema makes the shape a contract rather than a request, and validation closes the loop. Prompt requests (B), text parsing (C), and temperature (A) leave the shape to chance
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: How should a schema handle a value the source may not contain?

options.A: Omit the field silently
options.B: Supply a plausible default
options.C: Return an empty string in all cases
options.D: Define an explicit representation for absence

questions.rationale: Absence must be representable so a genuine gap is distinguishable from a failure. Silent omission (A) is ambiguous, a plausible default (B) fabricates, and an empty string (C) conflates absence with an empty value
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Extraction succeeds on typical inputs and fails on unusual ones. What is the most effective response?

options.A: Ask the model to be careful with unusual inputs
options.B: Use a larger model
options.C: Raise the temperature
options.D: Add examples covering the unusual formats and state what to return when a field is missing

questions.rationale: The unusual cases fail because they were never specified, and examples plus a missing-value rule specify them. Temperature (C) adds variance, model size (B) is not aimed at the gap, and exhortation (A) is not specification
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What is the clearest sign that a tool surface needs redesign rather than better prompting?

options.A: The model repeatedly selects a tool that cannot satisfy the request
options.B: It exposes more than five tools
options.C: The tools are implemented in different services
options.D: The tools return large payloads

questions.rationale: Repeated wrong selection indicates the tools are not distinguishable from their descriptions, which is a design fault. Tool count (B) and implementation topology (C) are not faults, and payload size (D) is a separate problem
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: How should a tool that deletes records be constrained?

options.A: By requiring more parameters
options.B: By enforcing authorisation and scope outside the model
options.C: By declaring it last among the tools
options.D: By a description warning the model to use it carefully

questions.rationale: Destructive capability is bounded by the surrounding system, since a description is a request rather than a control. Extra parameters (A) and ordering (C) do not limit authority
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: An MCP integration exposes an entire database through one general query tool. What is the architectural concern?

options.A: It uses too many tokens
options.B: The model's authority is unbounded, and least privilege cannot be applied
options.C: It cannot return structured output
options.D: It will be slow

questions.rationale: A single unrestricted tool removes the ability to scope what the model may reach. Speed (D) and tokens (A) are secondary, and structured output (C) is achievable either way
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Quality degrades steadily through a long agentic run. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The temperature is too low
options.B: Accumulated context has diluted the material that matters
options.C: The model version changed mid-run
options.D: The tools have become slower

questions.rationale: Progressive degradation over a long run is the signature of context accumulation. Versions do not change mid-run (C), low temperature (A) reduces variety rather than quality, and tool latency (D) does not affect correctness
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-2) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What must happen for state to survive a compaction boundary?

options.A: The context window must be enlarged
options.B: Nothing, the model retains what matters
options.C: The run must restart
options.D: The decisions and constraints that must persist are written into an explicit carried-forward summary

questions.rationale: Compaction is lossy, so persistence must be deliberate. Relying on recall (B) is unreliable, a larger window (A) only moves the boundary, and restarting (C) discards the work
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: An agentic design calls the same expensive tool repeatedly with identical arguments. What does this indicate?

options.A: The agent is not retaining or reusing the result, which points at the state design
options.B: The model is too capable
options.C: The tool is too fast
options.D: Healthy retry behavior

questions.rationale: Repeating an identical call means the prior result is not available to the agent, which is a state problem. It is not retry behavior (D), and neither tool speed (C) nor capability (B) explains it
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What determines whether two lines of work belong in separate subagents?

options.A: Whether each needs context the other would pollute
options.B: Whether they can run in parallel
options.C: Whether they use different tools
options.D: Their combined length

questions.rationale: Context isolation is the reason subagents exist. Length (D), tool difference (C), and parallelism (B) can all be handled within one context
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Which design most reduces the cost of a wrong autonomous decision?

options.A: Making the action reversible, or gating it behind confirmation
options.B: More tools
options.C: A longer prompt
options.D: A larger model

questions.rationale: Reversibility and gating bound the consequence, which is what the risk is. Capability (D), prompt length (C), and tools (B) affect the chance of error rather than its cost
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A CLAUDE.md has grown to several thousand lines. What is the likely effect?

options.A: Faster responses
options.B: The instructions that matter compete with material that no longer applies
options.C: No effect, since it is read once
options.D: Better results, because more context is available

questions.rationale: Project memory is context and dilutes like any other. More is not automatically better (D), it is not free (C), and it does not speed anything up (A)
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What should be true of a skill before it is committed to a shared repository?

options.A: It encodes a procedure the team genuinely repeats, and it is reviewable
options.B: It is long enough to be useful
options.C: It is written by the most senior engineer
options.D: It covers every edge case

questions.rationale: A shared skill is justified by genuine repetition and must be reviewable like code. Length (B), authorship (C), and exhaustiveness (D) do not establish that
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Why is committed configuration preferable to per-developer configuration for team conventions?

options.A: It uses less context
options.B: It is versioned, reviewed, and applies to everyone including automation
options.C: It cannot be overridden
options.D: It is faster to load

questions.rationale: Shared, reviewed, versioned context is what makes a convention hold across people and CI. Speed (D) and context size (A) are not the reason, and it can still be overridden locally (C)
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A schema-validated response fails validation once in every few hundred calls. What is the correct handling?

options.A: Ignore it, since the rate is low
options.B: Increase the output token limit
options.C: Disable validation to avoid the failures
options.D: Define a fallback path: retry, then fail explicitly rather than passing invalid data on

questions.rationale: A rare failure still needs a defined path, and silently passing invalid data is the outcome to prevent. Ignoring it (A) and disabling validation (C) do exactly that, and the token limit (B) is not the cause
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What is the advantage of validating structured output at the boundary rather than downstream?

options.A: It improves model accuracy
options.B: It is cheaper
options.C: It removes the need for a schema
options.D: The failure is caught where it can still be retried or rejected, before it contaminates later steps

questions.rationale: Catching at the boundary contains the fault. It is not primarily a cost question (B), the schema is what makes it possible (C), and it does not change the model's accuracy (A)
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A structured extraction must record where in the source each value came from. What does this require?

options.A: The schema to include a provenance field the model must populate
options.B: A longer prompt
options.C: A larger model
options.D: A second extraction pass

questions.rationale: Anything the output must carry has to be part of the declared shape. Model size (C) and prompt length (B) do not create a field, and a second pass (D) is unnecessary if the schema asks for it
