questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Two tools do nearly the same thing with different names. What is the architectural fault?

options.A: The model has no reliable basis for choosing between them
options.B: Duplication of code
options.C: Increased token cost
options.D: Higher latency

questions.rationale: Ambiguity at the point of selection is the fault, because the model chooses from descriptions. Code duplication (B), latency (D), and cost (C) are secondary consequences
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What should a tool do when given arguments it cannot satisfy?

options.A: Return a clear error stating what was wrong, so the model can correct the call
options.B: Return an empty result
options.C: Return the closest result it can
options.D: Raise an exception that terminates the run

questions.rationale: An informative error keeps the model able to adapt. A closest-guess (C) and an empty result (B) are silently wrong, and terminating (D) discards a recoverable run
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: An MCP tool exposes a write operation that the use case never needs. What should happen?

options.A: Rename it to discourage use
options.B: Leave it, since it may be useful later
options.C: Document that it should not be used
options.D: Remove it, because unused authority is unnecessary risk

questions.rationale: Authority that is not needed should not be granted. Retaining it for possible future use (B), documenting (C), or renaming (A) all leave the capability reachable
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: What is the earliest reliable signal that context management has failed in a long run?

options.A: Token cost rises
options.B: A tool returns an error
options.C: The run takes longer than expected
options.D: The agent begins repeating work or contradicting earlier decisions

questions.rationale: Repetition and self-contradiction are the behavioral signature of lost state. Duration (C) and cost (A) rise for many reasons, and a tool error (B) is unrelated
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: Why is a defined success criterion necessary for a reliable agentic system?

options.A: It makes the prompt shorter
options.B: It is required by the platform
options.C: It reduces token cost
options.D: Without it there is no way to tell completion from failure, so the system cannot stop correctly or be measured

questions.rationale: Termination and measurement both depend on a definition of done. Cost (C), prompt length (A), and platform requirements (B) are not the reason
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.source: Amey Thakur CLAUDE-CERTIFICATIONS repo (mock-3) | Warm-up (community, MIT)
questions.question: A reliability requirement says wrong output must never reach the user unnoticed. What does the design need?

options.A: A more capable model
options.B: A longer context window
options.C: A detection step with a defined action when it fires
options.D: More examples in the prompt

questions.rationale: Preventing silent error requires detection plus a response. Capability (A), examples (D), and context (B) improve the average case without catching the bad one
questions.label: Warm-up (community, MIT)

questions.question: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?

options.A: Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely
options.B: Log every update and deletion for later audit
options.C: Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
options.D: Restrict deletions to business hours

questions.rationale: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (B) and confirmations (C) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (D) narrows the window without closing it.

questions.question: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?

options.A: The temperature setting
options.B: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
options.C: The model, which may have degraded overnight
options.D: The system prompt wording

questions.rationale: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (C), unchanged prompt (D), and sampling (A) do not correlate with the refresh.

questions.question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

options.A: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
options.B: Limit the platform to ten capabilities
options.C: Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
options.D: One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors

questions.rationale: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (D) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (B) sacrifices the requirement.

questions.question: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

options.A: Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
options.B: A single fine-tuned model for both
options.C: One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
options.D: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents

questions.rationale: Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (D) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (C) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (B) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

questions.question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

options.A: Workflows always outperform agents
options.B: The team lacked time to build an agent
options.C: The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path
options.D: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general

questions.rationale: The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (D) and universal claims (A) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (B) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

questions.question: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?

options.A: Grade outputs by length
options.B: Ship and count complaints
options.C: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
options.D: Exact string match against one reference summary per clause

questions.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (D) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (A) measures nothing.

questions.question: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?

options.A: Roll it out; demos are representative
options.B: Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
options.C: Ask the team to vote
options.D: Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner

questions.rationale: Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

questions.question: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?

options.A: Blocking free-text queries entirely
options.B: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
options.C: A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
options.D: A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary

questions.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (B) is not a control, model instructions (C) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (A) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

questions.question: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?

options.A: Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit
options.B: Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
options.C: Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher
options.D: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap

questions.rationale: Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (D), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

questions.question: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?

options.A: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
options.B: Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
options.C: Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
options.D: Let each engineer keep personal settings only

questions.rationale: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

questions.question: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

options.A: The Claude API with request logging disabled
options.B: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
options.C: Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit
options.D: Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region

questions.rationale: A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (B), disabled logging (A), and transport encryption (C) all still involve the data leaving the account.

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
options.B: Let each team choose its own path
options.C: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
options.D: Use the Claude API and replicate the controls

questions.rationale: Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (C) creates a second control plane, replication (D) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (B) removes governance.

questions.question: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?

options.A: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place
options.B: It reduces token cost
options.C: It guarantees lower latency
options.D: It removes the need for evaluation

questions.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (B) or remove the need to evaluate (D), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

questions.question: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?

options.A: Increase the legacy timeout
options.B: Use the smallest model available
options.C: Force the model to answer within two seconds
options.D: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously

questions.rationale: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, C) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (A) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

questions.question: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?

options.A: Choosing the cheaper platform for both
options.B: Establishing which behaviors must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
options.C: Deploying to whichever region is nearest
options.D: Using identical prompts in both

questions.rationale: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (D) do not guarantee identical behavior, and cost (A) and proximity (C) do not address consistency.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?

options.A: The expected token cost
options.B: Which model to use
options.C: Whether the agent can be built in the available time
options.D: Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person

questions.rationale: Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (B), cost (A), and schedule (C) are all downstream of that boundary.

questions.question: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?

options.A: The more capable design, since capability is the point
options.B: The design with more components, for future flexibility
options.C: The design the team finds more interesting
options.D: Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity

questions.rationale: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (B) all pay that cost without justification.

questions.question: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?

options.A: Acceptable if a larger model is used
options.B: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.C: Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
options.D: Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator

questions.rationale: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behavior cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (C), disclosure (D), and model size (A) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

questions.question: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?

options.A: It has an evaluation suite
options.B: It includes a human approval step
options.C: Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
options.D: It uses more than one model

questions.rationale: Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (D), evaluation (A), and approval steps (B) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

questions.question: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?

options.A: A completed cost estimate
options.B: Agreement from the engineering team
options.C: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
options.D: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data

questions.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (C), consensus (B), and cost (A) do not establish whether the system works.

questions.question: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?

options.A: It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter
options.B: It is acceptable if it is large enough
options.C: It only matters for regulated systems
options.D: It gives a reliable measure of quality

questions.rationale: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (D), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

questions.question: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behavior. How is this best prevented?

options.A: Changing one thing at a time
options.B: Reviewing changes more carefully
options.C: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviors the system must not lose
options.D: Limiting how often prompts change

questions.rationale: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (A) and careful review (B) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

questions.question: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?

options.A: A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
options.B: A change in cost
options.C: A fixed annual schedule
options.D: Only a reported incident

questions.rationale: Any change to the things that determine behavior invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (D) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (B) does not affect correctness.

questions.question: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?

options.A: Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
options.B: Log responses only
options.C: Refuse, since logging creates risk
options.D: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence

questions.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (D) and blanket refusal (C) ignore one side, and a partial rule (B) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?

options.A: It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
options.B: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
options.C: It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content
options.D: It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel

questions.rationale: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (B) and prompt instructions (A) are bypassable, and transport security (D) says nothing about the content.

questions.question: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?

options.A: Nobody, since the output was automated
options.B: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.C: The organization that deployed the workflow
options.D: The model provider

questions.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (D) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (A).

questions.question: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?

options.A: Explain that quality cannot be summarised
options.B: Provide the model's benchmark score
options.C: Provide the headline accuracy figure
options.D: Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated

questions.rationale: A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (C) and a benchmark score (B) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (A) fails the sponsor.

questions.question: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: The training schedule
options.B: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
options.C: The cost of additional licenses
options.D: The need for a larger model

questions.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licenses (C), model size (D), and training (A) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

questions.question: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?

options.A: A longer warranty period
options.B: Full documentation at delivery
options.C: Training every user
options.D: A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update

questions.rationale: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (B) and training (C) age, and a warranty (A) covers defects rather than drift.

questions.question: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?

options.A: One model for everything, for simplicity
options.B: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
options.C: The largest model for everything, for safety
options.D: The newest model for everything

questions.rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (A, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?

options.A: A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.B: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
options.C: A limit that only matters for long documents
options.D: A setting to raise when quality drops

questions.rationale: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (B) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

questions.question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?

options.A: Move all prompts into the system prompt
options.B: Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
options.C: Appoint one team to own all prompting
options.D: Freeze the prompts

questions.rationale: Prompts that determine production behavior deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (C) may not fit the organization, freezing (D) blocks improvement, and relocation (A) does not address governance.

questions.question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?

options.A: Requiring approval for each use
options.B: A one-off training session
options.C: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
options.D: A written policy circulated by email

questions.rationale: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (D) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (A) creates friction without conveying practice.

questions.question: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement program is working?

options.A: License utilization
options.B: The number of people trained
options.C: The volume of tool calls
options.D: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve

questions.rationale: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilization (A), and activity (C) measure uptake rather than benefit.

questions.question: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?

options.A: Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
options.B: Whether a larger model would help
options.C: Whether the team needs more training
options.D: Whether the legacy service should be rewritten

questions.rationale: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (C) does not supply repository context, a larger model (B) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

questions.question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalog that changes daily. Which architecture fits?

options.A: An autonomous agent that browses the public website
options.B: Load the catalog into the system prompt
options.C: Fine-tune a model on the catalog nightly
options.D: Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalog changes, with the model answering from retrieved context

questions.rationale: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

questions.question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?

options.A: The model version
options.B: The generation prompt
options.C: Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently
options.D: The user interface

questions.rationale: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

questions.question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

options.A: Shorten all tool descriptions
options.B: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
options.C: Replace the agent with a larger model
options.D: Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools

questions.rationale: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

questions.question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?

options.A: A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
options.B: User thumbs-up counts alone
options.C: Exact match against reference summaries
options.D: Average output length compared to references

questions.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

questions.question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?

options.A: Ship it and monitor complaints
options.B: Team vote followed by rollout
options.C: Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
options.D: Rollout with a feedback form

questions.rationale: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

questions.question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?

options.A: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
options.B: Restricting the feature to structured queries only
options.C: A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing
options.D: A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI

questions.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

questions.question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?

options.A: Review only what users complain about
options.B: Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
options.C: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
options.D: Review every output regardless of risk

questions.rationale: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

questions.question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?

options.A: A refusal to quantify
options.B: An average weighted to look favorable
options.C: The highest observed number
options.D: Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review

questions.rationale: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

questions.question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?

options.A: The number of model providers
options.B: Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
options.C: The choice of programming language
options.D: Response latency targets

questions.rationale: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

questions.question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?

options.A: Workflows use less context
options.B: The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable
options.C: Agents cannot process documents
options.D: Workflows are always more accurate

questions.rationale: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

questions.question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?

options.A: Moving the preamble into a few-shot block
options.B: Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
options.C: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
options.D: Splitting the preamble across two requests

questions.rationale: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

questions.question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?

options.A: The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
options.B: The final design only
options.C: The implementation timeline
options.D: The team members involved

questions.rationale: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

questions.question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?

options.A: Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
options.B: Aggregate latency metrics only
options.C: Final outputs only
options.D: User feedback only

questions.rationale: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

questions.question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?

options.A: Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow
options.B: A shared chat channel
options.C: Individual coaching sessions
options.D: A recorded walkthrough

questions.rationale: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

questions.question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?

options.A: Logging modifications for later review
options.B: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
options.C: Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
options.D: Running the agent during business hours only

questions.rationale: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it

questions.question: A client requires that inference run inside their own AWS account. What does this determine?

options.A: The model family only
options.B: Deployment through Amazon Bedrock in the client's account and region
options.C: That request logging must be disabled
options.D: That a data processing agreement is sufficient

questions.rationale: Running inside the client's own cloud boundary is what the requirement describes. A contract (D) and logging settings (C) do not keep the data in the account, and the model family (A) is a separate choice

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud wants identity and audit handled by existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Use Bedrock for feature parity
options.B: Let each team decide
options.C: Use the Claude API and rebuild the controls
options.D: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply

questions.rationale: Aligning with the governed platform makes existing controls apply without duplication. Rebuilding (C) drifts, a different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, and per-team choice (B) removes governance

questions.question: What is the main architectural benefit of routing all model traffic through one internal service?

options.A: It removes the need for evaluation
options.B: Lower token prices
options.C: It guarantees lower latency
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are applied consistently in one place

questions.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once. It does not change unit price (B), remove evaluation (A), or reduce latency (C)

questions.question: Two designs both satisfy the requirement; one is materially simpler. What decides?

options.A: The more capable design, since headroom is valuable
options.B: The one with more components, for flexibility
options.C: Whichever the team prefers to build
options.D: Whether any stated requirement needs the extra capability, against the ongoing cost of complexity

questions.rationale: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Headroom (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (B) pay that cost without justification

questions.question: A required compliance control depends on the model behaving correctly. What is the correct judgment?

options.A: Not acceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.B: Acceptable with a documented residual risk
options.C: Acceptable if measured accuracy is very high
options.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

questions.rationale: A control that must hold needs a guarantee, which probabilistic behavior cannot supply. High accuracy (C), documentation (B), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee

questions.question: Where should the boundary of automation be drawn in a solution that makes customer-affecting decisions?

options.A: As far as the budget allows
options.B: At whatever the client requests
options.C: Wherever the model performs well in testing
options.D: Where accountability for the decision sits, keeping those decisions with a person

questions.rationale: Accountability determines what may be automated at all, and that boundary is an architectural decision. Test performance (C), budget (A), and unexamined requests (B) do not address responsibility

questions.question: What must exist before a solution is declared production-ready?

options.A: A completed cost model
options.B: A successful demonstration
options.C: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
options.D: Sign-off from the engineering team

questions.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar. A demonstration (B), consensus (D), and cost (A) do not establish whether it works

questions.question: An evaluation set contains only cases the system already handles. What is the effect?

options.A: It overstates performance and conceals the failures that matter
options.B: It is fine if it is large
options.C: It matters only in regulated contexts
options.D: It provides a reliable quality measure

questions.rationale: An unrepresentative sample measures the wrong distribution, and size does not correct bias. It is not reliable (D), scale does not fix it (B), and the problem is general (C)

questions.question: How should a request to log every prompt and response for audit be handled?

options.A: Decline, because logging creates risk
options.B: Establish what the audit requires, because prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
options.C: Implement it, since audit takes precedence
options.D: Log responses but not prompts

questions.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real, and the design must serve the audit purpose without retaining more than warranted. Blanket action (C) or refusal (A) ignores one side, and an arbitrary split (D) is unjustified

questions.question: Who is accountable when an automated Claude workflow produces a harmful decision?

options.A: The model provider
options.B: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.C: The organization that deployed it
options.D: No one, because the decision was automated

questions.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes. The provider (A) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D)

questions.question: A sponsor asks for one number that shows whether the solution is working. What is the right response?

options.A: Explain that this cannot be reduced to a number
options.B: Give the model's benchmark score
options.C: Give the headline accuracy figure
options.D: Give the measure tied to the decision they face, and state what it does not cover

questions.rationale: A useful metric matches the decision and is honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (C) and a benchmark (B) can mislead, and refusing (A) fails the sponsor

questions.question: A ten-user pilot is about to expand to two thousand users. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: Whether a larger model is needed
options.B: License cost
options.C: The training rollout plan
options.D: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand

questions.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and surfacing those is the architect's contribution. Cost (B), model size (A), and training (C) follow from knowing what breaks

questions.question: How should a model be chosen for a solution containing several distinct tasks?

options.A: The newest model everywhere
options.B: One model everywhere, for simplicity
options.C: The largest model everywhere, for safety
options.D: Match each task to the smallest model meeting its requirement, and evaluate the choices

questions.rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate on evidence. Uniform choices (A, B, C) optimise for convenience rather than fit

questions.question: How should the context window be treated in a production design?

options.A: As a budget allocated deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.B: As a setting to increase whenever quality drops
options.C: As a concern only for long documents
options.D: As capacity to fill as completely as possible

questions.rationale: Context is scarce and its allocation drives quality, so it is designed. Filling it (D) dilutes, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (B) does not fix allocation

questions.question: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across dozens of repositories. What is most durable?

options.A: A policy document circulated once
options.B: Requiring approval for every use
options.C: A single training session
options.D: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code

questions.rationale: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (C) fade, and per-use approval (B) adds friction without conveying practice

questions.question: A client will not accept a solution whose behavior cannot be explained to their auditor. What does this constrain?

options.A: The model family only
options.B: The deployment region
options.C: The architecture, which must make decisions traceable and the controls inspectable
options.D: The cost model

questions.rationale: Auditability is an architectural property covering tracing and inspectable controls. Model family (A), cost (D), and region (B) do not by themselves make behavior explicable

questions.question: What is the main risk of building directly against a single cloud's model service with no abstraction?

options.A: Moving later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
options.B: Higher token cost
options.C: Slower responses
options.D: Lower accuracy

questions.rationale: Coupling determines the cost of change, which is the architectural concern. Cost (B), accuracy (D), and latency (C) are not consequences of the coupling itself

questions.question: A solution must serve users in two regions with different data residency rules. What follows?

options.A: Whichever region has the lowest latency
options.B: Separate deployments whose data stays within each region's boundary
options.C: One deployment in the cheaper region
options.D: A single deployment with encryption in transit

questions.rationale: Residency is satisfied by keeping the data within each boundary. A single deployment (C, D) moves data across it, and latency (A) does not address the rule

questions.question: A requirement is stated as make it as accurate as possible. What should the architect do?

options.A: Establish the accuracy the use case actually needs and what an error costs
options.B: Build the most complex design the budget allows
options.C: Defer the question until after the pilot
options.D: Choose the largest model and optimise from there

questions.rationale: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be made concrete. Defaulting to maximum capability (B, D) spends without a target, and deferring (C) leaves the design unanchored

questions.question: Two components each work correctly but the system fails intermittently at their boundary. What does this suggest?

options.A: The contract between them is underspecified, particularly for edge and error cases
options.B: The failure is transient and can be retried
options.C: One component needs a larger model
options.D: The system needs more components

questions.rationale: Boundary failures between correct components point at the contract. Capability (C) and more components (D) do not define the interface, and retrying (B) hides it

questions.question: A design proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely. What should the architect raise?

options.A: Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations retention creates
options.B: That storage is expensive
options.C: That it will slow the system
options.D: Nothing, retention is always safer

questions.rationale: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it. Treating retention as free of risk (D) is the error, and cost (B) and speed (C) are minor by comparison

questions.question: How should a solution handle the case where the model is confident and wrong?

options.A: Ask the model to double-check
options.B: Design so that consequential outputs are verified against something independent of the model
options.C: Use two models and take the agreement
options.D: Trust the confidence signal

questions.rationale: Independence is what catches confident error. Confidence (D) is not evidence, self-checking (A) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (C)

questions.question: An evaluation shows 94% accuracy. What else must be known before this is actionable?

options.A: The token cost of the evaluation
options.B: The model version only
options.C: What the 6% look like, and what each failure costs
options.D: How long the evaluation took

questions.rationale: A headline rate is only meaningful alongside the shape and cost of the failures. Version (B), cost (A), and duration (D) do not describe the risk

questions.question: What should happen when a model version is updated beneath a production solution?

options.A: Roll back automatically if complaints rise
options.B: Nothing, versions are compatible
options.C: Re-run the evaluation suite before the change reaches production traffic
options.D: Increase monitoring for a week

questions.rationale: A change to the thing that determines behavior invalidates prior measurement. Assuming compatibility (B) is unsafe, and monitoring (D) or reacting to complaints (A) detects after users are affected

questions.question: A stakeholder asks why the solution cannot simply be fully automated. What is the most useful answer?

options.A: That the budget does not allow it
options.B: That automation is always risky
options.C: Which specific decisions carry accountability or are unverifiable, and what automating them would risk
options.D: That the technology is not ready

questions.rationale: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited. Generic claims about readiness (D) or risk (B) are not, and budget (A) is not the reason

questions.question: What should be handed over with a solution so it survives its first year?

options.A: The source code
options.B: The evaluation suite, the criteria, the owner, and the routine for re-checking
options.C: A list of prompts used
options.D: A recorded demonstration

questions.rationale: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain, with someone responsible. Code (A), a demonstration (D), and prompts (C) are artefacts without the means to verify them

questions.question: A team reports the solution has become worse, but nothing was deployed. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The inputs or the surrounding usage changed
options.B: The evaluation was wrong originally
options.C: The prompts wore out
options.D: The model degraded on its own

questions.rationale: Behavior changes with what is fed to it, and distribution drift is the usual cause. Models do not degrade unprompted (D), prompts do not wear out (C), and the original evaluation is not the first suspect (B)

questions.question: How should prompts that determine production behavior be managed?

options.A: Edited in place when someone notices a problem
options.B: Kept in a shared document for easy editing
options.C: Frozen after launch
options.D: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on change, like code

questions.rationale: Anything that determines production behavior needs the lifecycle of code. Ad hoc edits (A) and open documents (B) invite unreviewed change, and freezing (C) blocks improvement

questions.question: An organization asks how to measure whether Claude Code is worth the license cost. What should be measured?

options.A: Hours spent in the tool
options.B: Number of tool invocations
options.C: Change in the delivery outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
options.D: Number of users onboarded

questions.rationale: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated. Invocations (B), onboarding (D), and time in tool (A) measure usage rather than benefit

questions.question: What most often blocks a team from getting good results from Claude Code on an existing codebase?

options.A: The number of contributors
options.B: The absence of committed context describing the conventions and structure
options.C: The programming language
options.D: The size of the repository

questions.rationale: Missing project context is the usual cause, and it is the one the team can fix. Size (D), language (C), and contributor count (A) do not by themselves prevent good results
